title: I've been pouring my heart into this FPS game. Here's how it's looking so far.
author: Sweet-Chip6849
selftext:
I've been putting so much of my time and energy into this game lately, and I honestly just wanted to share it with more people.

It's called FLOW FIRE BODYCAM.

I'm building it with AI agents, mainly Claude Opus and DeepSeek. I guide the development, explain exactly what I'm trying to achieve, provide references, test everything myself, and keep pushing things until they feel right. The AI handles the technical implementation, supported by testing tools we've been building along the way.

What excites me the most is seeing how much the game changes with every iteration. Sometimes I look at footage from just a few days ago and can't believe the difference.

There's still a lot I want to improve, especially the animations and how everything feels during gameplay. But I'm genuinely enjoying this process.

This clip is actual gameplay, and it recently passed 1,000 views on YouTube. That might not sound like much to some people, but seeing others discover something I've been working so hard on means a lot to me.

I'd genuinely love to hear what you think, especially what stands out to you or what you think could be improved.

Thanks for checking it out!

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
I get your point now, and I appreciate the heads-up!

Just to clarify, I'm not using their code, assets, or game content. FLOW FIRE is being developed independently in Godot, with its own systems and mechanics.

But you're right that trademark rights are a separate issue. I'll look into the naming carefully, especially since I eventually want to commercialize the game.

Thanks for pointing that out, genuinely!

comments.author: Such-Improvement-605
comments.body:
you are headed straight into a brick wall in my opinion.

As an indie dev, you will most likely never get good and realistic visuals (unless your bodycam but thats a whole different tech demo we dont need to get into) which it seems that you are trying to hit.

We humans are very good at identifying unrealistic movements and fooling them takes a lot of work. you need motion capture and all that expensive stuff.. thats why indie games usually have a style to them.

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
I actually agree with you about how hard realistic human movement is. It's probably one of the biggest challenges I've faced so far haha.

But that's also what makes this project so interesting to me. I'm not just generating animations and hoping they look right. I've been building tools to analyze movement frame by frame, compare results, and keep refining the physics and animation systems.

I'm also using existing animation resources as a foundation, combined with procedural reactions and physics.

I'm definitely not claiming I've solved realism yet. I'm just really curious to see how far I can push it as an indie developer working with AI. And honestly, the progress over the last few days has been pretty crazy!

replies.author: Such-Improvement-605
replies.body:
Wish you the best! Im also quite interested in learning about animation and potentially inverse kinematics and such but haven gotten to it yet.

Its also good because once you get that down you can adventure into cool and unique movements like all those spider monsters and stuff

comments.author: Sweet-Chip6849
comments.body:
Mostly Claude Opus and DeepSeek, but the most interesting part is probably the custom testing system we've been building haha.

I direct the development, provide references, explain the results I'm looking for, and make the final decisions. The AI agents handle the technical implementation.

We've built our own tools using Python, Godot, and Blender to capture gameplay, compare before/after footage, and measure things like camera movement, weapon behavior, physics, and enemy reactions.

So it's not just prompting an AI to make a game. A lot of the work goes into evaluating what it creates and figuring out why something doesn't feel right.

Still improving the whole workflow every day! 🔥

I use a similar flow, usually spending a majority of the time defining a GDD, providing and designing on photoshop and having huge asset libraries both acquired and created manually. It's ain't much but it's honest work.

comments.author: United-Objective2149
comments.body: No offense but this looks like Temu Bodycam

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
Yeah, and I really appreciate your honesty! I genuinely love people who give honest feedback like that.

This video is actually a bit outdated compared to where the game is right now. I've completely reworked the graphics and improved the visual quality quite a lot. The animations are also much more natural than what you see in this video, although I'm still constantly refining and improving them.

Thanks to the engine I built, I feel like the development process has improved massively. It really makes a huge difference compared to not having it, saves me a ton of tokens, and has honestly made animation development so much faster.

But seriously, I really appreciate your honesty. And you're absolutely right about the camera. It still needs a lot of work, especially when it comes to filters and visual effects.

It's tricky trying to maintain a consistently high level of visual quality while keeping the game well optimized, but I'm confident I can achieve something pretty decent without sacrificing performance.

Thanks again for the genuine feedback! I really appreciate it.

replies.author: Sweet-Chip6849
replies.body:
I get your point, bro, but I'm not trying to plagiarize any game. My game is inspired by Bodycam, but it's aimed at a much smaller niche.

The video I posted is already pretty far behind where Flow Fire is today. Every single day, the game gets more refined than it was the day before.

And about AI, this is where I strongly disagree with you. AI is an incredibly powerful tool if you know what you're doing, how to direct it, what tools to have it build, and how to guide the whole process.

There's a huge difference between blindly accepting everything AI generates or tells you and actually reviewing, questioning, and evaluating its work with your own knowledge and judgment.

I know how to code, and I'm not new to this. I just find it pretty inefficient to criticize people for using AI when directing it properly can save an enormous amount of time and effort compared to doing everything yourself.

Obviously, AI has its limitations, but that's exactly something I've been working hard on. I've built a separate evaluation engine to help overcome those limitations and continuously improve the results when working with AI.

I still appreciate your honesty and the fact that you're willing to express your opinion openly. Seriously, that's something I genuinely value. I respect people who speak their minds and tell the truth, even when we disagree.

But just to put your mind at ease, Flow Fire isn't going to be plagiarism or some cheap copy of another game.

My goal is to offer the best experience I possibly can without requiring people to have an insanely powerful PC just to play comfortably.
